- Root: ط-ب-ع (ṭ-b-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes imprinting, stamping, and the innate disposition (ṭabʿ) of a thing; also the natural constitution (ṭabīʿah) as that which is impressed upon a body.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological discourse, ṭabīʿah is the created order of causes and effects — not an autonomous agent, but a subjugated instrument (musakhkharah) of the Creator.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage refers to the physical stamp or seal; metaphorically, it denotes the inherent character of a thing. Here, Ghazali employs it in the literal sense of natural bodies, while denying them independent agency.
- Root: س-خ-ر (s-kh-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To subjugate, compel, or employ for service; the subjugated (musakhkhar) is that which acts not by its own will but by another's command.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Quranic idiom, taskhīr denotes the divine ordering of the heavens, earth, and all within them as servants to humanity and signs of God's power — never as self-acting entities.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: to force into service. Metaphorical: the cosmic bodies are described as "subjugated" (musakhkharāt) — a ḥaqīqah of divine decree, not a majāz of mere influence.
- Root: ج-س-د (j-s-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The body (jasad) as opposed to the spirit (rūḥ); corporeal substance extended in space.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In eschatological discourse, the resurrection of bodies (ḥashr al-ajsād) is a matter of revealed truth (samʿ), affirming bodily reward and punishment alongside spiritual recompense.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical embodiment. The philosophers' claim of purely spiritual reward is a metaphorical reduction (majāz) that denies the literal truth of the Quranic descriptions.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Exception and Restriction (al-istithnāʾ wa al-ḥaṣr) — In the phrase "إلا في مسائل معينة" (except in certain specific questions), the exception clause restricts the general permission, requiring the translator to preserve the precise scope of the author's concession.
chapters.translation:
### | 3 —

As for the natural sciences (al-ṭabīʿiyyāt): it is an inquiry into the world of the heavens and their celestial bodies, and what lies beneath them of the simple bodies (al-ajsām al-mufradah) — such as water, air, earth, and fire — and into the composite bodies (al-ajsām al-murakkabah), such as the animal, the plant, and the mineral; and into the causes of their transformation and intermixture. In this, it closely parallels the science of medicine (al-ṭibb) concerning the human body, its principal and servient organs, and the causes of the alteration of its temperament (mizāj). And just as it is not a condition of religion to deny the science of medicine, so too is it not a condition of it to deny that science — except in certain specific questions, which we have mentioned in the book *The Incoherence of the Philosophers* (Tahāfut al-Falāsifah). Whatever else they must be opposed in is, upon reflection, seen to be subsumed under those questions. The sum and root of all of them is this: that you know that nature (al-ṭabīʿah) is subjugated (musakhkharah) to God Most High — it does not act by itself, but rather is employed by its Originator (fāṭirihā). The sun, the moon, the stars, and the natural dispositions (al-ṭabāʾiʿ) are all subjugated by His command; no one of them has any act by its own essence, from its own essence.

### | 4 —

As for the divine sciences (al-ilāhiyyāt): in them lies the greater part of their errors. For they were unable to fulfill the demonstrations (barāhīn) according to the conditions they themselves had stipulated in logic; and for this reason disagreement among them multiplied therein. Indeed, the doctrine of Aristotle (Arisṭāṭālīs) therein came close to the doctrines of the Muslims — according to what al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā have transmitted — but the totality of what they erred in reduces to twenty principles (aṣlan). We must declare them unbelievers (takfīr) in three of them, and innovators (tabdīʿ) in seventeen. For the refutation of their doctrine in these twenty questions, we composed the book *The Incoherence*. As for the three questions, they have therein opposed all the Muslims — namely, in their saying:

1. That bodies shall not be resurrected (lā tuḥshar), and that only the disembodied spirits (al-arwāḥ al-mujarradah) are rewarded and punished; and that the rewards and punishments are spiritual (rūḥāniyyah), not corporeal (jismāniyyah).

And indeed they spoke truly in affirming the spiritual — for it too shall certainly come to be — but they lied in denying the corporeal, and committed unbelief against the Sacred Law (al-sharīʿah) in what they uttered.

### | 2 —

And of that is their saying: "God Most High knows universals (al-kulliyyāt) but not particulars (al-juzʾiyyāt)." This too is outright unbelief (kufr ṣarīḥ). Rather, the truth is that {«لَا يَعْزُبُ عَنْهُ مِثْقَالُ ذَرَّةٍ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَلَا فِي الْأَرْضِ»} — "There escapes Him not the weight of an atom in the heavens nor in the earth" (Q. 34:3).

### | 3 —

And of that is their saying: that the world is eternal (qadīm) and pre-eternal (azalī). And no one among the Muslims has gone to any of these questions.

As for what lies beyond that — their denial of the [divine] attributes (al-ṣifāt), and their saying that He is knowing by His essence (ʿalīm bi-al-dhāt) and does not know anything additional to the essence, and what runs in that vein — their doctrine therein is close to the doctrine of the Muʿtazilah, and it is not obligatory to declare the Muʿtazilah unbelievers for the like of that. And we have mentioned in the book *The Criterion of Distinction Between Islam and Heresy* (Fayṣal al-Tafriqah bayn al-Islām wa al-Zandaqah) that by which is made clear the corruption of the view of one who hastens to declare unbelief (takfīr) against everything that opposes his own doctrine.

### | 5 —

As for the political sciences (al-siyāsiyyāt): all their speech therein reduces to prudential judgments (al-ḥikam al-maṣlaḥiyyah) pertaining to worldly affairs and royal governance (al-iyālah al-sulṭāniyyah). And they have taken this only from the Books of God revealed upon the prophets, and from the wise sayings transmitted from the predecessors of the prophets — peace be upon them.

### | 6 —

As for the ethical sciences (al-khuluqiyyah): all their speech therein reduces to the enumeration of the attributes of the soul (ṣifāt al-nafs) and its character traits (akhlāquhā), the mention of their genera and species, and the manner of their treatment and combat (muʿālajatihā wa-mujāhadatihā). And they have taken this only from the speech of the Sufis (al-ṣūfiyyah) — who are the devotees of God (al-mutaʾallihūn), the persevering in the remembrance of God Most High (dhikr Allāh), and in opposing caprice (al-hawā), and in traversing the path to God Most High by turning away from the pleasures of this world. And there was disclosed to them, in their spiritual striving (mujāhadatihim), of the character traits of people and their defects, and the afflictions of their deeds, that which they made explicit. The philosophers took this, and mixed it with their own speech, seeking by adorning themselves with it to promote their falsehood (bāṭiluhum). And indeed there were in their age — nay, in every age — a company of the devotees of God; God — glory be to Him — does not leave the world devoid of them, for they are the pegs of the earth (awtād al-arḍ); by their blessings mercy descends upon the people of the earth, as has come in the report (al-khabar), where he — may God's peace and blessing be upon him — said: "By them you are given rain, and by them you are provided sustenance" (bihim tumṭarūn, wa-bihim turzaqūn). And of them were the Companions of the Cave (aṣḥāb al-kahf), who were in bygone ages, according to what the Quran has declared.

So there was generated, from their mixing of the speech of prophecy and the speech of the Sufis with their own books, two afflictions (āfah): an affliction with respect to the one who accepts [them], and an affliction with respect to the one who rejects [them].

chapters.title_en: Section 7 — On the Grave Harm of Rejecting Truth Due to Its Source
chapters.arabic_text:
### | 1 -

أما الآفة التي في حق الراد فعظيمة: إذ ظنت طائفة من الضعفاء أن ذلك
الكلام إذا كان مدونا في كتبهم، وممزوجا بباطلهم، ينبغي أن يهجر ولا يذكر
بل ينكر على كل من يذكره إذ لم يسمعوه أولا منهم، فسبق إلى عقولهم الضعيفة
أنه باطل، لأن قائله مبطل، كالذي يسمع من النصراني قوله: " لا إله إلا
الله، عيسى رسول الله " فينكره ويقول: " هذا كلام النصارى "، ولا يتوقف
ربما يتأمل أن النصراني كافر باعتبار هذا القول، أو باعتبار إنكاره نبوة
محمد عليه الصلاة والسلام. فإن لم يكن كافرا إلا باعتبار إنكاره، ينبغي أن
يخالف في غير  ما هو به كافر مما هو حق في نفسه، وإن كان أيضا حقا عنده.
وهذه عادة ضعفاء العقول، يعرفون الحق بالرجال، لا الرجال بالحق. والعاقل
يقتدي بقول أمير المؤمنين " علي بن أبي طالب " رضي الله عنه، حيث قال: لا
تعرف الحق بالرجال بل اعرف الحق تعرف أهله،
والعارف العاقل يعرف الحق، ثم ينظر في نفس القول: فإن كان حقا قبله سواء
كان قائله مبطلا أو محقا، بل ربما يحرص على انتزاع الحق من تضاعيف كلام أهل
الضلال، عالما بأن معدن الذهب الرغام. ولا بأس على الصراف إن أدخل يده في
كيس القلاب وانتزع الإبريز الخالص من الزيف والبهرج. مهما كان واثقا
ببصيرته، ويمنع - من ساحل البحر - الأخرق، دون السباح الحاذق، ويصد عن مس
الحية الصبي دون المعزم البارع. ولعمري! لما غلب على أكثر الخلق ظنهم
بأنفسهم الحذاقة والبراعة وكمال العقل، وتمام الآلة في تمييز الحق عن
الباطل والهدى عن الضلال وجب حسم الباب في زجر الكافة عن مطالعة كتب أهل
الضلال ما أمكن، إذ لا يسلمون عن الآفة الثانية التي سنذكرها أصلا، وإن
سلموا عن هذه الآفة التي ذكرناها. ولقد اعترض - على بعض الكلمات المبثوثة
في تصانيفنا في أسرار علوم الدين - طائفة من الذين لم تستحكم في العلوم
سرائرهم، ولم تنفتح إلى أقصى غايات المذاهب بصائرهم،
وزعمت أن تلك الكلمات من كلام الأوائل، مع أن بعضها من مولدات الخواطر،
ولا يبعد أن يقع الحافر على الحافر، وبعضها يوجد في الكتب الشرعية، وأكثرها
موجود معناه في كتب الصوفية، وهب أنها لم توجد إلا في كتبهم، فإذا كان ذلك
الكلام معقولا في نفسه، مؤيدا بالبرهان ولم يكن على مخالفة الكتاب والسنة،
فلم ينبغي أن يهجر ويترك؟! فلو فتحنا هذا الباب، وتطرقنا إلى أن يهجر كل حق
سبق إليه خاطر مبطل، للزمنا أن نهجر كثيرا من الحق، ولزمنا أن نهجر جملة
آيات من آيات القرآن وأخبار الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم وحكايات السلف،
وكلمات الحكماء والصوفية لأن صاحب إخوان الصفا أوردها في كتابه  مستشهدا بها
ومستدرجا قلوب الحمقى بواسطتها إلى باطل، ويتداعى ذلك إلى أن يستخرج
المبطلون الحق من أيدينا بإيداعهم إياه كتبهم. وأقل درجات العالم: أن يتميز
عن العامي الغمر.
فلا يعاف
العسل، وإن وجده في محجمة الحجام، ويتحقق أن المحجمة لا تغير ذات العسل،
فإن نفرة الطبع عنه مبنية على جهل عامي منشؤه أن المحجمة إنما صنعت للدم
المستقذر، فيظن أن الدم مستقذر لكونه في المحجمة، ولا يدري أنه مستقذر لصفة
في ذاته، فإذا عدمت هذه الصفة في العسل، فكونه في ظرفه لا يكسبه تلك الصفة،
فلا ينبغي أن يوجب له الاستقذار، وهذا وهم باطل، وهو غالب على أكثر الخلق.
فإذا نسبت الكلام وأسندته إلى قائل حسن فيه اعتقادهم، قبلوه وإن كان باطلا،
وإن أسندته إلى من ساء فيه اعتقادهم ردوه وإن كان حقا، فأبدا يعرفون الحق
بالرجال ولا يعرفون الرجال بالحق، وهو غاية الضلال! هذه آفة الرد.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-د-د (r-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To return, repel, reject; the act of turning something back upon its source.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Intellectual rejection (radd) of a proposition based on its attributed origin, not its intrinsic validity — a failure of discernment (tamyīz).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical repulsion; metaphorical (majāz) — epistemic dismissal of truth due to prejudice against the speaker.
- Root: ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Established reality, truth, that which is due and certain.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Truth as ontological correspondence with reality (muṭābaqah), independent of the moral status of its utterer.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — fixed, verified fact; metaphorical — the act of "extracting" truth from falsehood's matrix, as gold from ore.
- Root: ذ-ه-ب (dh-h-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Gold; to go, depart.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Pure gold (dhahab) as symbol of incorruptible essence, unaffected by its container.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the metal; metaphorical — truth's intrinsic purity, immune to external contamination.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Law/La- (امتناع لامتناع) — The protasis (law) and apodosis (la-) express a counterfactual causal nexus, used here to demonstrate that rejecting truth on account of its source would logically entail abandoning the Qur'an and Sunnah themselves.
chapters.translation:
As for the affliction that befalls the one who rejects [such discourse], it is grave indeed. For a group of the weak-minded supposed that when such speech is recorded in their books and intermingled with their falsehood, it must be shunned and never mentioned — nay, one must condemn anyone who mentions it, simply because they had not first heard it from them. Thus it rushed into their feeble intellects that it is false, because its speaker is a falsifier. This is like one who hears a Christian say: "There is no god but God, and Jesus is the Messenger of God," and so rejects it, saying: "This is Christian speech," without pausing to reflect whether the Christian is an unbeliever by virtue of this utterance, or by virtue of his denial of Muhammad's prophethood (peace and blessing be upon him). For if he is an unbeliever only by virtue of that denial, then one should oppose him in that wherein he is an unbeliever — not in what is true in itself, even if it is also true in his view.

This is the habit of weak intellects: they know truth by men, not men by truth. But the wise man follows the saying of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may God be pleased with him), where he said: "Do not know truth by men; rather, know the truth, and you will know its people." The knowing and wise man recognizes truth, then looks at the utterance itself: if it is true, he accepts it — whether its speaker is a falsifier or a verifier. Indeed, he may even strive to extract truth from the folds of the speech of the people of error, knowing that the mine of gold is dust. And there is no harm for the money-changer if he plunges his hand into the purse of the counterfeiter and draws out the pure gold (ibrīz) from the dross and the alloyed — so long as he is confident in his discernment. But the clumsy one is barred from the seashore, while the skilled swimmer is not; and the child is kept from touching the serpent, while the adept exorcist is not.

By my life! Since the majority of mankind have been overcome by the delusion that they possess skill, proficiency, complete intellect, and perfect instruments for distinguishing truth from falsehood and guidance from error, it became necessary to seal the door — as far as possible — in restraining the common folk from studying the books of the people of error. For they are not safe from the second affliction which we shall mention at all, even if they are safe from this first affliction we have now discussed.

Indeed, a group of those whose inner depths in the sciences had not been solidified, and whose insights had not opened to the furthest ends of the schools [of thought], objected to certain words scattered in our compositions concerning the secrets of the science of religion. They claimed that those words were from the speech of the Ancients (al-awāʾil) — though some of them were original products of [our own] reflections, and it is not unlikely that one footfall should fall upon another's footfall. Some of them are found in the scriptural books, and most of their meanings are found in the books of the Sufis. But grant that they are found only in their books — if that speech is rational in itself, supported by demonstration, and not in opposition to the Book and the Sunnah, then why should it be shunned and abandoned?!

If we were to open this door, and proceed to abandon every truth that a falsifier's thought had previously reached, then we would be compelled to abandon much of the truth. We would be compelled to abandon whole verses of the Qur'an, reports of the Messenger (peace and blessing be upon him), narratives of the Salaf, and sayings of the sages and Sufis — because the author of the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity (Ikhwān al-Ṣafā) cited them in his book, using them as evidence and thereby luring the hearts of fools to falsehood. And this would lead to the falsifiers extracting the truth from our hands by the mere fact of their depositing it in their books.

The least degree of the scholar is that he be distinguished from the raw commoner. So let him not loathe honey, even if he finds it in the cupping-glass of the blood-letter. Let him realize that the cupping-glass does not alter the substance of the honey. For the aversion of the natural temperament to it is based on an ignorant, common error: its origin is that the cupping-glass is made for loathsome blood, so one supposes that the blood is loathsome because it is in the cupping-glass — not knowing that it is loathsome for a quality in its own essence. When that quality is absent in the honey, its being in that vessel does not acquire that quality for it, and so it should not render it loathsome. This is a false illusion, and it dominates most of mankind.

Thus, when you attribute speech and ascribe it to a person in whom their belief is good, they accept it — even if it is false. And when you ascribe it to one in whom their belief is bad, they reject it — even if it is true. So they always know truth by men, and do not know men by truth — and this is the extreme of error! This is the affliction of rejection.

chapters.title_en: The Second Malady: The Malady of Acceptance — On the Danger of Philosophical Works and the Duty of the Learned
chapters.arabic_text:
### | 2 -

والآفة الثانية آفة القبول: فإن من نظر في كتبهم كإخوان الصفا وغيره،
فرأى ما مزجوه بكلامهم من الحكم النبوية، والكلمات الصوفية، ربما استحسنها
وقبلها، وحسن اعتقاده فيها، فيسارع إلى قبول باطلهم الممزوج به لحسن ظنه
مما رآه استحسنه، وذلك نوع استدراج إلى الباطل.
ولأجل هذه الآفة يجب الزجر عن مطالعة كتبهم لما فيها من الغدر والخطر.
وكما يجب صون من لا يحسن السباحة على مزالق الشطوط، يجب صون الخلق عن
مطالعة تلك الكتب. وكما يجب صون الصبيان عن مس الحيات، يجب صون الأسماع عن
مختلط الكلمات، وكما يجب على المعزم أن لا يمس الحية بين يدي ولده الطفل،
إذا علم أن سيقتدي به ويظن أنه مثله، بل يجب عليه أن يحذره منه، بأن يحذر
هو في نفسه ولا يمسها بين يديه، فكذلك يجب على العالم الراسخ مثله، وكما أن
المعزم الحاذق إذا أخذ الحية وميز بني الترياق والسم، واستخرج منها الترياق
وأبطل السم، فليس له أن يشح بالترياق على المحتاج إليه. وكذا الصراف الناقد
البصير إذا أدخل يده في كيس القلاب، وأخرج  منه الإبريز الخالص، وطرح الزيف
والبهرج، فليس له أن يشح بالجيد المرضي على من يحتاج إليه، فكذلك العالم.
وكما أن المحتاج إلى الترياق، إذا اشمأزت نفسه منه، حيث علم أنه مستخرج من
الحية التي هي مركز السم وجب تعريفه، والفقير المضطر إلى المال، إذا نفر عن
قبول الذهب المستخرج
من كيس القلاب، وجب تنبيهه على أن نفرته جهل محض، هو سبب حرمانه الفائدة
التي هي مطلبه، وتحتم تعريفه أن قرب الجوار بين الزيف والجيد لا يجعل الجيد
زيفا، كما لا يجعل الزيف جيدا، فكذلك قرب الجوار بين الحق الباطل، لا يجعل
الحق باطلا، كما لا يجعل الباطل حقا، فهذا مقدار ما أردنا ذكره من آفة
الفلسفة وغائلتها.

### | مذهب التعليم وغائلته
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ب-ل (q-b-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To receive, accept, take willingly; also "to come forward" — implying an active movement of the soul toward what is offered.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Acceptance (qabūl) as a moral-psychological act — the heart's inclination toward a claim, distinct from mere intellectual assent; here it denotes uncritical receptivity born of prior approval.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: taking something in hand. Metaphorical (majāz): the soul's embrace of an idea; the phrase "acceptance of falsehood" (qabūl al-bāṭil) is a metaphor for being ensnared by what is mixed with truth.
- Root: غ-ر-ر (gh-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deception, heedlessness, being lured; also "white blaze on a horse's forehead" — a mark that misleads the eye.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Gradual enticement (istidrāj) — divine or human leading astray by degrees, where each step seems harmless until the trap closes.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a state of being unmindful. Metaphorical: "the deception of the world" (ghurūr al-dunyā) — that which appears beneficial but is ruinous.
- Root: ز-ي-ف (z-y-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Counterfeit coin; to be false, spurious; also "to incline away" — the deviation of a thing from its true standard.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, the counterfeit (zayf) is that which mimics truth in form but lacks its substance — parallel to bāṭil (falsehood) that wears the garment of ḥaqq (truth).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: debased metal. Metaphorical: false doctrine presented with the rhetoric of truth — the "mixing" (khalṭ) of prophetic wisdom with philosophical error.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Conditional of Analogy (al-sharṭ al-tamthīlī) — In the sentence "As it is obligatory to guard the non-swimmer from slippery riverbanks, so it is obligatory to guard creation from reading those books," the particle "kamā" (just as) introduces a protasis whose apodosis is governed by an implicit qiyās (analogical inference). The structure demands that the listener transfer the ruling from the known case (the child, the non-swimmer) to the unknown (the unlearned reader), establishing a binding legal-ethical parallel.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second malady is the malady of acceptance. For whoever looks into their books — such as the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity (Ikhwān al-Ṣafā) and others — and sees what they have blended into their discourse of prophetic wisdom and Sufi sayings, may well find it admirable and accept it, and his belief in it becomes good. Thus he hastens to accept their falsehood that is mixed with it, due to his good opinion of what he saw and admired. And that is a kind of gradual enticement (istidrāj) toward falsehood.

It is on account of this malady that one must sternly forbid the study of their books, because of the treachery and peril they contain. And just as it is obligatory to guard the one who does not know how to swim from the slippery edges of riverbanks, so it is obligatory to guard the common people from reading those books. And just as it is obligatory to guard children from touching serpents, so it is obligatory to guard ears from the mixed words [of the philosophers]. And just as it is incumbent upon the spell-charmer not to touch the serpent in the presence of his young child — when he knows that the child will imitate him and think himself his equal — nay, rather he must warn the child against it by himself being wary and not touching it before him — so likewise is it incumbent upon the deeply rooted scholar (al-ʿālim al-rāsikh). And just as the skilled spell-charmer, when he seizes the serpent and distinguishes between the antidote (tiryāq) and the venom, extracting the antidote from it and nullifying the venom — it is not for him to withhold the antidote from the one who needs it. And likewise, the discerning, sharp-eyed money-changer, when he plunges his hand into the purse of the counterfeiter and draws out the pure gold (ibrīz), casting away the debased and the spurious — it is not for him to withhold the good and approved from the one who needs it. So too is the scholar.

And just as the one who needs the antidote, when his soul recoils from it upon learning that it is extracted from the serpent which is the seat of the venom, must be informed [of its benefit], and the poor man compelled by need for wealth, when he shrinks from accepting gold extracted from the counterfeiter's purse, must be alerted that his aversion is sheer ignorance — the very cause of his being deprived of the benefit that is his goal — and it is incumbent to inform him that the proximity of the counterfeit to the good does not make the good counterfeit, just as it does not make the counterfeit good. So too, the proximity of truth to falsehood does not make truth falsehood, just as it does not make falsehood truth. This, then, is the extent of what we intended to mention concerning the malady of philosophy and its perilous consequence.

chapters.title_en: The Investigation of the Taʿlīmiyyah (Bāṭiniyyah) and the Futility of Their Doctrine
chapters.arabic_text:
ثم إني لما فرغت من علم الفلسفة وتحصيله وتفهمه وتزييف ما يزيف منه، علمت
أن ذلك أيضا غير واف بكمال الغرض، وأن العقل ليس مستقلا بالإحاطة بجميع
المطالب، ولا كاشفا للغطاء عن جميع المعضلات، وكان قد نبغت نابغة
التعليمية، وشاع بني الخلق تحدثهم بمعرفة معنى الأمور من جهة الإمام
المعصوم القائم بالحق، فعن لي أن أبحث في مقالاتهم، لأطلع على ما في
كنانتهم. ثم اتفق أن ورد علي أمر جازم من حضرة الخلافة، بتصنيف كتاب يكشف
عن حقيقة مذهبهم. فلم يسعني مدافعته، وصار ذلك مستحثا من خارج، ضميمة
للباعث من الباطن، فابتدأت بطلب كتبهم وجمع مقالاتهم. وكذلك قد بلغني بعض
كلماتهم المستحدثة التي ولدتها خواطر أهل العصر، لا على المنهاج المعهود من
سلفهم. فجمعت تلك الكلمات، ورتبتها ترتيبا محكما مقارنا للتحقيق، واستوفيت
الجواب عنها، حتى أنكر بعض أهل الحق مبالغتي في تقرير حجتهم، فقال: هذا سعي
لهم، فإنهم كانوا
يعجزون عن نصرة مذهبهم بمثل هذه الشبهات لولا تحقيقك لها، وترتيبك إياها.
وهذا الإنكار من وجه حق، فقد أنكر أحمد بن حنبل على الحارث المحاسبي رحمهما
الله تصنيفه في الرد على المعتزلة، فقال الحارث: الرد على البدعة فرض فقال
أحمد: نعم، ولكن حكيت شبهتهم أولا ثم أجبت عنها، فيم تأمن أن
يطالع الشبهة من يعلق ذلك بفهمه، ولا يلتفت إلى الجواب أو ينظر في الجواب
ولا يفهم كنه؟
وما ذكره أحمد بن حنبل حق، ولكن في شبهة لم تنتشر ولم تشتهر فأما إذا
انتشرت، فالجواب عنها واجب ولا يمكن الجواب عنها إلا بعد الحكاية. نعم،
ينبغي أن لا يتكلف لهم شبهة لم يتكلفوها، ولم أتكلف أنا ذلك، بل كنت قد
سمعت تلك الشبهة من واحد من أصحابي المختلفين إلي، بعد أن كان قد التحق
بهم، وانتحل مذهبهم، وحكى أنهم يضحكون على تصانيف المصنفين في الرد عليهم،
بأنهم لم يفهموا بعد حجتهم، ثم ذكر تلك الحجة وحكاها عنهم، فلم أرض لنفسي
أن يظن في الغفلة عن اصل حجتهم، فلذلك أوردتها، ولا أن يظن بي أني - وإن
سمعتها - لم أفهمها، فلذلك قررتها.
والمقصود، أني قررت شبهتهم إلى أقصى الإمكان ثم أظهرت فسادها بغاية
البرهان.
والحاصل: أنه لا حاصل عند هؤلاء ولا طائل لكلامهم، ولولا سوء نصرة الصديق
الجاهل، لما انتهت تلك البدعة - مع ضعفها - إلى هذه الدرجة، ولكن شدة
التعصب دعت الذابين عن الحق إلى تطويل النزاع معهم في مقدمات كلامهم، وإلى
مجاحدتهم في كل ما نطقوا به، فجاحدوهم
في دعواهم: الحاجة إلى التعليم والمعلم، وفي دعواهم أنه: لا يصلح كل
معلم، بل لا بد من معلم معصوم وظهرت حجتهم في إظهار الحاجة إلى التعليم
والمعلم، وضعف قول المنكرين في مقابلته، فاغتر بذلك جماعة وظنوا أن ذلك من
قوة مذهبهم وضعف مذهب المخالفين، ولم يفهموا أن ذلك لضعف ناصر الحق وجعله
بطريقه، بل الصواب الاعتراف بالحاجة إلى المعلم، وأنه لا بد وأن يكون
المعلم معصوما، ولكن معلمنا المعصوم هو محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم فإذا
قالوا: هو ميت فنقول: ومعلمكم غائب فإذا قالوا: معلمنا قد علم الدعاة وبثهم
في البلاد، وهو ينتظر مراجعتهم إن اختلفوا أو أشكل عليهم مشكل فنقول:
ومعلمنا قد علم الدعاة وبثهم في البلاد وأكمل التعليم إذ قال الله تعالى: "
اليوم أكملت لكم دينكم وأتممت عليكم نعمتي "، وبعد كمال التعليم  لا يضر موت
المعلم كما لا يضر غيبته.
فبقي قولهم: كيف تحكمون فيما لم تسمعوه؟ أبالنص ولم تسمعوه، أم بالإجتهاد
والرأي وهو مظنة الخلاف؟ فنقول: نفعل ما فعله معاذ إذ بعثه رسول الله عليه
الصلاة
والسلام إلى اليمن. أن نحكم بالنص عند وجود النص، وبالإجتهاد عند عدمه.
بل كما يفعله دعاتهم إذا بعدوا عن الإمام إلى أقاصي البلاد إذ لا يمكنه أن
يحكم بالنص، فإن النصوص المتناهية لا تستوعب الوقائع الغير المتناهية، ولا
يمكنه الرجوع في كل واقعة إلى بلدة الإمام، وأن يقطع المسافة ويرجع فيكون
المستفتي قد مات، وفات الانتفاع بالرجوع، فمن أشكلت عليه القبلة ليس له
طريق إلا أن يصلي بالاجتهاد، إذ لو سافر إلى بلدة الإمام لمعرفة القبلة،
فيفوت وقت الصلاة. فإذن، جازت الصلاة إلى غير القبلة بناء على الظن. ويقال:
إن المخطيء في الاجتهاد له أجر واحد وللمصيب أجران فكذلك في جميع
المجتهدات،
وكذلك أمر صرف الزكاة إلى الفقير، فربما يظنه فقيرا باجتهاده وهو غني
باطنا بإخفائه ماله، فلا يكون مؤاخذا به وإن أخطأ، لأنه لم يؤاخذ إلا بموجب
ظنه. فإن قال: ظن مخالفه كظنه فأقول: هو مأمور باتباع ظن نفسه، كالمجتهد في
القبلة يتبع ظنه وإن خالفه غيره فإن قال: فالمقلد يتبع أبا حنيفة والشافعي
رحمهما الله أم غيرهما؟ فأقول: فالمقلد في القبلة عند الاشتباه في معرفة
الأفضل الأعلم بدلائل القبلة، فيتبع ذلك الاجتهاد، فكذلك في المذاهب فرد
الخلق إلى الاجتهاد - ضرورة - الأنبياء والأئمة مع العلم بأنهم قد يخطئون،
بل قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:
" أنا أحكم بالظاهر والله يتولى السرائر ". أي أنا أحكم بغالب الظن
الحاصل من قول الشهود، وربما أخطأوا فيه. ولا سبيل إلى الأمن من الخطأ
للأنبياء في مثل هذه المجتهدات فيكف يطمع في ذلك؟.
ولهم ها هنا سؤالان: أحدهما قولهم: هذا وإن صح في المجتهدات فلا يصح في
قواعد العقائد، إذ المخطئ فيه غير معذور، فكيف السبيل إليه؟ فأقول: قواعد
العقائد يشتمل عليها الكتاب والسنة، وما وراء ذلك من  التفصيل، والمتنازع
فيه، يعرف الحق فيه بالقسطاس المستقيم. وهي الموازين التي ذكرها الله تعالى
في كتابه، وهي خمسة ذكرتها في كتاب القسطاس المستقيم " فإن قال: خصومك
يخالفونك في ذلك الميزان فأقول: ولا يتصور أن يفهم ذلك الميزان ثم يخالف
فيه، إذ لا يخالف فيه أهل التعليم، لأني استخرجته من القرآن وتعلمته منه،
ولا يخالف فيه أهل المنطق، لأنه موافق لما شرطوه في المنطق وغير مخالف له،
ولا يخالف فيه المتكلم لأنه موافق لما يذكره في أدلة النظريات، وبه يعرف
الحق في الكلاميات. فإن قال: فإن كان في يدك مثل هذا الميزان فلم لا ترفع
الخلاف بين الخلق؟، فأقول: لو أصغوا إلي لرفعت الخلاف بينهم،
وذكرت طريق رفع الخلاف في كتاب القسطاس المستقيم فتأمله لتعلم أنه حق
وأنه يرفع الخلاف قطعا لو أصغوا ولا يصغون إليه بأجمعهم! بل قد أصغى إلي
طائفة، فرفعت الخلاف بينهم.
وإمامك يريد رفع الخلاف بينهم مع عدم إصغائهم، فلم لم يرفع إلى الآن؟ ولم
لم يرفع علي رضي الله عنه وهو رأس الأئمة؟ أو يدعي أنه يقدر على حمل كافتهم
على الإصغاء قهرا، فلم لم يحملهم إلى الآن؟ ولأي يوم أجله؟ وهل حصل بين
الخلق بسبب دعوته إلا زيادة خلاف وزيادة مخالف؟ نعم! كان يخشى من الخلاف
نوع الضرر لا ينتهي إلى سفك الدماء، وتخريب البلاد وأيتام الأولاد، وقطع
الطرق، والإغارة على الأموال. وقد حدث في العالم من بركات رفعكم الخلاف من
الخلاف ما لم يكن بمثله عهد. فإن قال: ادعيت أنك ترفع الخلاف بين الخلق
ولكن المتحير بين المذاهب المتعارضة، والاختلافات المتقابلة، لم يلزمه
الإصغاء إليك دون خصمك وأكثر الخصوم يخالفونك، ولا فرق بينك وبينهم وهذا هو
سؤالهم الثاني، فأقول: وهذا أولا ينقلب عليك، فإنك إذا دعوت هذا المتحير
إلى نفسك فيقول المتحير: بما صرت أولى من مخالفيك، وأكثر أهل العلم
يخالفونك؟ فليت شعري! بماذا تجيب؟ أتجيب بأن تقول: إمامي منصوص عليه، فمن
يصدقك في دعوى النص، وهو لم يسمع النص من الرسول؟ وإنما يسمع  دعواك مع
تطابق أهل العلم على اختراعك وتكذيبك. ثم هب أنه سلم لك النص، فإن كان
متحيرا في أصل النبوة، فقال: هب أن إمامك يدلي بمعجزة عيسى عليه السلام
فيقول: الدليل على صدقي أني أحيي أباك، فأحياه، فناطقني بأنه محق، فبماذا
أعلم صدقه؟ ولم يعلم كافة الخلق صدق عيسى عليه السلام بهذه المعجزة، بل
عليه من الأسئلة المشكلة ما لا يدفع إلا بدقيق النظر العقلي، والنظر العقلي
لا يوثق به عندك، ولا يعرف دلالة المعجزة على الصدق ما لم يعرف السحر
والتمييز بينه وبين المعجزة، وما لم يعرف أن الله لا يضل عباده. وسؤال
الإضلال وعسر تحرير الجواب عنه مشهور فبماذا تدفع جميع ذلك؟ ولم يكن إمامك
أولى بالمتابعة من مخالفه! فيرجع إلى الأدلة النظرية التي ينكرها، وخصمه
يدلي بمثل تلك الأدلة وأوضح منها وهذا السؤال قد انقلب عليهم انقلابا عظيما
لو اجتمع أولهم وآخرهم على أن يجيبوا عنه جوابا لم يقدروا عليه. وإنما نشأ
الفساد من جماعة من الضعفة ناظروهم، فلم يشتغلوا
بالقلب بل بالجواب. وذلك مما يطول فيه الكلام، وما لا يسبق سريعا إلى
الإفهام، فلا يصلح للإفحام. فإن قال قائل: فهذا هو القلب، فهل عنه جواب؟
فأقول: نعم! جوابه أن المتحير لو قال: أنا متحير ولم يعين المسألة التي هو
متحير فيها، يقال له: أنت كمريض، يقول: أنا مريض ولا يعين مرضه ويطلب علاجه
فيقال له: ليس في الوجود علاج للمرض المطلق، بل لمرض معين. من صداع أو
إسهال أو غيرهما فكذلك المتحير ينبغي أن يعين ما هو متحير فيه، فإن عين
المسألة عرفته الحق فيها بالوزن بالموازين الخمسة، التي لا يفهمها أحد إلا
ويعترف بأنه الميزان الحق، ويفهم منه أيضا صحة الوزن، كما يفهم متعلم علم
الحساب، نفس الحساب، وكون المحاسب المعلم عالما بالحساب وصادقا فيه. وقد
أوضحت ذلك في كتاب القسطاس المستقيم في مقدار عشرين ورقة، فليتأمل.
وليس المقصود الآن بيان فساد مذهبهم، فقد ذكرت ذلك في كتاب المستظهري
أولا، وفي كتاب حجة الحق ثانيا،  وهو جواب كلام لهم عرض علي ببغداد،
وفي كتاب مفصل الخلاف الذي هو اثنا عشر فصلا ثالثا، وهو جواب كلام عرض
علي بهمدان، وفي كتاب الدرجة المرقوم بالجداول رابعا، وهو من ركيك كلامهم
الذي عرض علي بطوس، وفي كتاب القسطاس المستقيم خامسا، وهو كتاب مستقل
مقصوده أن هؤلاء، ليس معهم شيء من الشفاء المنجي من ظلمات الآراء، بل هم مع
عجزهم عن إقامة البرهان على تعيين الإمام، طالما جربناهم فصدقناهم في
الحاجة إلى التعليم، وإلى المعلم المعصوم وعرضنا عليهم إشكالات فلم
يفهموها، فضلا عن القيام بحلها! فلما عجزوا أحالوا على الإمام الغائب،
وقالوا: إنه لا بد من السفر إليه والعجب أنهم ضيعوا عمرهم في طلب المعلم
وفي التبجح بالظفر به، ولم يتعلموا منه شيئا أصلا، كالمتضمخ بالنجاسة، يتعب
في طلب الماء حتى إذا وجده لم يستعمله، وبقي متضمخا بالخبائث. ومنهم من
ادعى شيئا من علمهم، فكان حاصل ما ذكره شيئا من
ركيك فلسفة فيثاغورس وهو رجل من قدماء الأوائل، ومذهبه أرك مذهب الفلسفة،
وقد رد عليه أرسطاطاليس، بل استدرك كلامه واسترذله، وهو المحكي في كتاب
إخوان الصفا وهو على التحقيق حشو الفلسفة.
فالعجب ممن يتعب طول العمر في تحصيل العلم ثم يقنع بمثل ذلك العلم الركيك
المستغيث، ويظن بأنه ظفر بأقصى مقاصد العلوم! فهؤلاء أيضا جربناهم وسبرنا
ظاهرهم وباطنهم، في رجع حاصلهم إلى استدراج العوام، وضعفاء العقول ببيان
الحاجة إلى المعلم، ومجادلتهم في إنكارهم الحاجة إلى التعليم بكلام قوي
مفحم، حتى إذا ساعدهم على الحاجة إلى المعلم مساعد وقال: هات علمه وأفدنا
من تعليمه! وقف وقال: الآن إذا سلمت لي هذا فاطلبه، فإنما غرضي هذا القدر
فقط. إذ علم أنه لو زاد على ذلك لافتضح ولعجز عن حل أدنى الإشكالات، بل عجز
عن فهمه، فضلا عن جوابه. فهذه حقيقة حالهم فأخبرهم تقلهم فلما جربناهم
نفضنا اليد عنهم أيضا.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ب-غ (n-b-gh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To spring forth, to gush out (of water); to emerge suddenly and become prominent.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Emergence of something novel that surpasses its peers; used here for the sudden appearance of a new sect.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for water springing; metaphorical for a person or idea rising abruptly into prominence.
- Root: ك-ن-ن (k-n-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cover, conceal, shelter; the "كنانة" is the quiver (covering for arrows).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The inner hidden reality of a doctrine; what is concealed within one's breast or arsenal of arguments.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal covering; metaphorical for the hidden depths of a school's teachings.
- Root: ق-س-ط (q-s-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Justice, equity; the "قسطاس" is the balance or scale.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The just balance of rational and revealed proof; the epistemological criterion for truth.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal weighing instrument; metaphorical for the logical and theological method of adjudicating truth.
- Root: د-ر-ج (d-r-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To ascend step by step; a "درجة" is a step, degree, or rank.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Gradual progression in knowledge or station; here, the title of a book (al-Darajah) indicating graded levels of argument.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal stair-step; metaphorical for levels of proof or stages of inquiry.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Responsive Constructions (الشّرط والجزاء) — The frequent use of "فإن قال... فقولوا/فأقول" (If they say... then we say) structures the dialectical exchange as a formal disputation, with the protasis (condition) and apodosis (response) strictly governed by the rules of ʿaṭf and jazm, ensuring logical sequence and rhetorical force.
chapters.translation:
I say: When I had completed the science of philosophy — its acquisition, comprehension, and the refutation of what therein deserved refutation — I knew that this too was insufficient for the complete attainment of the goal, and that the intellect is not independent in encompassing all objects of inquiry, nor does it lift the veil from all perplexities. Now, there had sprung forth a new sprout, the Taʿlīmiyyah (the Bāṭiniyyah), and their talk spread among the people — that the meaning of things is known only from the infallible Imam, the one established upon the truth. So it occurred to me to investigate their doctrines, in order to discover what lay within their quiver (kanānah).

Then it so happened that a decisive command came to me from the presence of the Caliphate, ordering me to compose a book that would uncover the reality of their sect. I could not evade it, and this became an external impetus, joined to the internal motive. So I began to seek out their books and to collect their doctrines. Likewise, some of their newly-invented sayings reached me — sayings born of the fancies of the people of this age, not following the well-trodden path of their predecessors. I gathered these sayings, arranged them in a firm order commensurate with verification, and exhausted the answers to them — until some of the people of truth censured my excess in setting forth their argument, saying: "This is aiding them! For they would be incapable of defending their doctrine with such doubts were it not for your verification of them and your arrangement of them."

This censure is in one respect true. For Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal (may Allah have mercy on him) censured al-Ḥārith al-Muḥāsibī (may Allah have mercy on him) for composing his book in refutation of the Muʿtazilah. Al-Ḥārith said: "Refuting innovation is an obligation." Aḥmad replied: "Yes, but you first narrated their doubt and then answered it. How can you be secure that one who reads the doubt — and it clings to his understanding — will not neglect the answer, or look at the answer but fail to grasp its essence?"

What Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal mentioned is true — but regarding a doubt that has not spread nor become notorious. As for a doubt that has spread, answering it is obligatory, and it cannot be answered except after narrating it. Indeed, one should not fabricate for them a doubt they themselves did not fabricate. And I did not fabricate such. Rather, I had heard that doubt from one of my companions who used to visit me, after he had joined them and adopted their sect. He narrated that they laugh at the compositions of those who write refutations against them, saying: "They have not even understood our argument." Then he mentioned that argument and narrated it from them. I was not pleased that it should be thought of me that I was heedless of the root of their argument — therefore I presented it. Nor that it should be thought of me that I — even if I heard it — did not understand it — therefore I set it forth fully.

The point is: I set forth their doubt to the utmost possible extent, then I demonstrated its corruption with the utmost proof.

The sum of it: There is no substance to these people, and no profit in their speech. Were it not for the evil advocacy of the ignorant friend, that innovation — despite its weakness — would not have reached this degree. But intense partisanship drove the defenders of truth to prolong the dispute with them over the premises of their discourse, and to obstinately deny them in everything they uttered. So they denied them their claim of the need for instruction (taʿlīm) and a teacher (muʿallim), and their claim that not every teacher suffices, but rather an infallible teacher is necessary. Their argument became manifest in demonstrating the need for instruction and a teacher, and the weakness of the deniers' position in opposition to it. A group was thereby deceived, thinking that this indicated the strength of their doctrine and the weakness of their opponents' — not understanding that it was due to the weakness of the defender of truth and his faulty method. Rather, the correct course is to acknowledge the need for a teacher, and that the teacher must be infallible. But our infallible teacher is Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him). If they say: "He is dead," we say: "And your teacher is absent." If they say: "Our teacher has taught his callers and dispatched them throughout the lands, and he awaits their return if they differ or a difficulty confronts them," we say: "Our teacher has taught his callers and dispatched them throughout the lands, and completed the instruction — for Allah the Exalted said: {«اليوم أكملت لكم دينكم وأتممت عليكم نعمتي»} ('This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you')." After the completion of instruction, the death of the teacher does no harm, just as his absence does no harm.

Then remains their saying: "How do you judge matters you have not heard? By a text (naṣṣ) you have not heard, or by ijtihād and opinion, which is a locus of disagreement?" We say: We do what Muʿādh did when the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) sent him to Yemen — we judge by the text when the text exists, and by ijtihād when it does not. Indeed, this is what their own callers do when they are far from the Imam in the remotest lands, for he cannot judge by the text — since the finite texts do not encompass the infinite occurrences — nor can he return in every matter to the Imam's city, traversing the distance and coming back, for the questioner would have died and the benefit of return would be lost. Whoever is perplexed about the qiblah has no way but to pray by ijtihād, for if he traveled to the Imam's city to learn the qiblah, the time of prayer would pass. Thus, praying toward other than the qiblah based on predominant conjecture (ẓann) is permissible. It is said: The one who errs in ijtihād has one reward, and the one who is correct has two. Likewise in all matters of ijtihād. Similarly, the matter of disbursing zakāh to the poor — one might deem a person poor by his ijtihād while he is secretly wealthy, having hidden his property; he is not held accountable for that even if he erred, for he is only held accountable according to what his conjecture dictates.

If they say: "The conjecture of one who disagrees is like his conjecture," I say: He is commanded to follow his own conjecture, like the one who exercises ijtihād regarding the qiblah — he follows his conjecture even if others disagree with him. If they say: "Then does the muqallid (follower) follow Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on them) or others?" I say: The muqallid regarding the qiblah, when the directions are confused, follows the one most excellent and most knowledgeable in the evidences of the qiblah, and follows that ijtihād. Likewise in the schools of law. Thus, the people are referred — by necessity — to ijtihād, as are the prophets and imams, with the knowledge that they may err. Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "I judge by the apparent, and Allah takes charge of the inner secrets" — meaning: I judge by the predominant conjecture arising from the testimony of witnesses, and they might err in it. There is no way to be secure from error for the prophets in such matters of ijtihād — so how can one aspire to that?

They have two questions here. The first is their saying: "This, even if valid in matters of ijtihād, is not valid in the foundations of creed (ʿaqāʾid), for the one who errs therein is not excused. How then is the path to it?" I say: The foundations of creed are encompassed by the Book and the Sunnah. As for what lies beyond that — the details and the disputed matters — the truth therein is known by the Straight Balance (al-Qisṭās al-Mustaqīm). These are the balances that Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book, and they are five, which I have mentioned in my book al-Qisṭās al-Mustaqīm.

If they say: "Your opponents disagree with you regarding that balance," I say: It is inconceivable that one understands that balance and then disagrees with it. For the people of Taʿlīm do not disagree with it, because I extracted it from the Qurʾān and learned it from it. The people of logic do not disagree with it, because it conforms to what they stipulated in logic and does not contradict it. The theologians (mutakallimūn) do not disagree with it, because it conforms to what they mention in the evidences of theoretical matters, and by it the truth is known in theological questions.

If they say: "If you possess such a balance, why do you not remove the disagreement among the people?" I say: If they would listen to me, I would remove the disagreement among them. I have mentioned the way of removing disagreement in the book al-Qisṭās al-Mustaqīm — examine it, and you will know that it is true and that it would remove disagreement definitively, if they would listen. But they will not all listen! Indeed, a group has listened to me, and I removed the disagreement among them.

And your Imam wishes to remove disagreement among them despite their not listening — why has he not removed it until now? And why did ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), the head of the imams, not remove it? Or does he claim that he can compel them all to listen by force — why has he not compelled them until now? For what day is he waiting? Has anything resulted among the people from his call except increased disagreement and increased opposition? Indeed! Before, disagreement was feared as a type of harm that did not reach the shedding of blood, the ruination of lands, the orphaning of children, the cutting of roads, and the raiding of wealth. But from the blessings of your removal of disagreement, there has occurred in the world a disagreement the like of which was never seen in an age.

If they say: "You claim that you remove disagreement among the people, but the one perplexed between conflicting schools and opposing differences is not obliged to listen to you rather than your opponent — and most opponents disagree with you, and there is no difference between you and them." This is their second question. I say: This first turns back upon you. For if you call this perplexed one to yourself, he says: "How have you become more worthy than your opponents, when most of the people of knowledge disagree with you?" By my life! How would you answer? Would you answer by saying: "My Imam is explicitly designated (manṣūṣ ʿalayh)"? But who would believe you in your claim of designation, when he has not heard the designation from the Messenger? He only hears your claim, along with the agreement of the people of knowledge that you have fabricated it and that you lie. Then, even if he grants you the designation — if he is perplexed about the very foundation of prophethood, he says: "Suppose your Imam performs a miracle like that of Jesus (peace be upon him) — he says: 'The proof of my truthfulness is that I revive your father,' and he revives him, and he speaks to me that he is right. How do I know his truthfulness?" The entirety of creation did not know the truthfulness of Jesus (peace be upon him) through this miracle alone. Rather, upon him are difficult questions that cannot be repelled except by subtle rational inquiry — and rational inquiry is not trusted by you, nor is the indication of the miracle to truthfulness known without knowing sorcery and distinguishing between it and the miracle, nor without knowing that Allah does not mislead His servants. And the question of misguidance (iḍlāl) and the difficulty of formulating an answer to it is well-known. How do you repel all of that? Your Imam is not more worthy of being followed than his opponent! So it returns to the rational evidences that he denies — and his opponent adduces similar evidences, and clearer ones.

This question has turned back upon them with a mighty reversal. If their first and last gathered to answer it, they could not. The corruption arose only from a group of weak ones who debated them and did not occupy themselves with the counter-attack (qalb), but rather with mere answering. This is a matter that would prolong speech, and what does not quickly reach the understanding is not suitable for silencing (ifḥām).

If someone says: "This is the counter-attack (qalb) — is there an answer to it?" I say: Yes! Its answer is that if the perplexed one says: "I am perplexed," without specifying the question in which he is perplexed, one says to him: You are like a sick man who says: "I am sick," without specifying his illness, and seeks treatment. One says to him: There is no treatment in existence for absolute sickness, but rather for a specific sickness — a headache, diarrhea, or other than that. Likewise, the perplexed one must specify that in which he is perplexed. If he specifies the question, I will show him the truth therein by weighing it with the five balances — which no one understands except that he acknowledges it as the true balance, and understands from it the soundness of the weighing, just as the learner of arithmetic understands the arithmetic itself, and that the teacher who teaches arithmetic is knowledgeable in it and truthful in it. I have clarified this in the book al-Qisṭās al-Mustaqīm in about twenty folios — let him examine it.

The present purpose is not to demonstrate the corruption of their doctrine — I have mentioned that in the book al-Mustaẓhirī first, and in the book Ḥujjat al-Ḥaqq second (which is an answer to a discourse of theirs presented to me in Baghdad), and in the book Mufaṣṣal al-Khilāf, which is twelve chapters, third (an answer to a discourse presented to me in Hamadān), and in the book al-Darajah al-Marqūmah bi-al-Jadāwil fourth (from the feeble speech of theirs presented to me in Ṭūs), and in the book al-Qisṭās al-Mustaqīm fifth (an independent book). The purpose is that these people possess nothing of the healing that saves from the darknesses of opinions. Rather, despite their incapacity to establish proof for the designation of the Imam, we have long tested them — we affirmed them in the need for instruction and for the infallible teacher, and we presented to them difficulties which they did not understand, let alone rise to solving! When they were incapacitated, they referred to the absent Imam, saying: "One must travel to him." The wonder is that they wasted their lives in seeking the teacher and in boasting of having found him, yet they learned nothing from him at all — like one smeared with filth who exhausts himself seeking water, and when he finds it, does not use it, remaining smeared with impurities.

Among them is one who claimed something of their knowledge, and the sum of what he mentioned was something of the feeble philosophy of Pythagoras — a man among the ancient predecessors, whose doctrine is the feeblest of philosophical doctrines. Aristotle refuted him — indeed, he corrected his speech and deemed it base. It is what is narrated in the book Ikhwān al-Ṣafā, and in truth it is the filler (ḥashw) of philosophy.

The wonder is at one who exhausts his entire life in acquiring knowledge, then is satisfied with such feeble, crying-out-for-help knowledge, and thinks he has attained the utmost aims of the sciences! These too — we have tested them and probed their outward and inward. The sum of their result is the enticement of the common folk and the weak-minded by demonstrating the need for a teacher, and their disputation against those who deny the need for instruction with strong, silencing speech — until when one agrees with them on the need for a teacher and says: "Bring his knowledge and benefit us from his instruction!" they stop and say: "Now that you have conceded this to me, seek it yourself — my aim was only this much." For they know that if they went beyond that, they would be exposed and incapable of solving the least of difficulties — indeed, incapable of understanding it, let alone answering it. This is the reality of their state — so inform them of their paucity. When we tested them, we washed our hands of them as well.

chapters.title_en: The Paths of the Sufis (Ṭuruq al-Ṣūfiyyah)
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ر-ق (ṭ-r-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes a path, way, or road—specifically one that is beaten, trodden, or traversed repeatedly; also a "striking" (as in a knock at the door), implying a persistent seeking.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, ṭarīqah refers to a method or spiritual discipline leading to knowledge of God—distinct from mere intellectual speculation (naẓar), emphasizing praxis and experiential striving.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = a physical road; metaphorical (majāz) = a spiritual method or school of conduct, as in "the path of the Sufis" (ṭarīqat al-ṣūfiyyah), indicating a collective way of life.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʾIḍāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase "طرق الصوفية" is a construct state (muḍāf ilayh), where "طرق" (paths) is indefinite plural and "الصوفية" (the Sufis) is definite, yielding "the paths of the Sufis"—signifying multiple distinct yet unified approaches within a single tradition.

chapters.arabic_text:
ثم إني لما فرغت من هذه العلوم أقبلت بهمتي على طريق الصوفية، وعلمت أن
طريقتهم إنا تتم بعلم وعمل، وكان  حاصل علومهم قطع عقبات النفس، والتنزه عن
أخلاقها المذمومة وصفاتها الخبيثة، حتى يتوصل بها إلى تخلية القلب عن غير
الله تعالى وتحليته بذكر الله.
وكان العلم أيسر علي من العمل، فابتدأت بتحصيل علمهم من مطالعة كتبهم
مثل: قوت القلوب لأبي طالب المكي رحمه الله، وكتب الحارث المحاسبي،
والمتفرقات المأثورة عن الجنيد
والشبلي وأبي يزيد البسطامي قدس الله أرواحهم وغيرهم من المشايخ، حتى
اطلعت على كنه مقاصدهم العلمية، وحصلت ما يمكن أن يحصل من طريقهم بالتعلم
والسماع. فظهر لي أن
أخص خواصهم، ما لا يمكن الوصول إليه بالتعلم بل بالذوق والحال وتبدل
الصفات. وكم من الفرق أن تعلم حد الصحة وحد الشبع وأسبابهما وشروطهما، وبين
أن تكون صحيحا وشبعان؟ وبين أن تعرف حد السكر، وأنه عبارة عن حالة تحصل من
استيلاء أبخرة تتصاعد من المعدة على معادن الفكر، وبين أن تكون سكران! بل
السكران لا يعرف حد السكر، وعلمه وهو سكران وما معه من علمه شيء. الطبيب في
حالة المرض يعرف حد الصحة وأسبابها وأدويتها، وهو فاقد الصحة. فكذلك فرق
بين أن تعرف حقيقة الزهد وشروطه وأسبابه، وبين أن تكون حالك الزهد، وعزوف
النفس عن الدنيا!.
فعلمت يقينا أنهم أرباب الأحوال، لا أصحاب الأقوال. وأن ما يمكن تحصيله
بطريق العلم فقد حصلته، ولم يبق إلا ما لا سبيل إليه بالسماع والتعلم، بل
بالذوق والسلوك. وكان قد حصل معي - من العلوم التي مارستها والمسالك التي
سلكتها، في التفتيش عن صنفي العلوم الشرعية والعقلية إيمان يقيني
بالله تعالى، وبالنبوة، وباليوم الآخر.
فهذه الأصول الثلاثة من الإيمان كانت قد رسخت في نفسي، لا بدليل معين
مجرد، بل بأسباب وقرائن وتجارب لا تدخل تحت الحصر تفاصيلها. وكان قد ظهر
عندي أنه لا مطمع لي في سعادة الآخرة إلا بالتقوى، وكف النفس عن الهوى، وأن
رأس ذلك كله، قطع علاقة القلب عن الدنيا، بالتجافي عن دار الغرور، والإنابة
إلى دار الخلود، والإقبال بكنه الهمة على الله تعالى. وأن ذلك لا يتم إلا
بالإعراض عن الجاه والمال،  والهرب من الشواغل والعلائق. ثم لاحظت أحوالي،
فإذا أنا منغمس في العلائق، وقد أحدقت بي من الجوانب، ولاحظت أعمالي -
وأحسنها التدريس والتعليم - فإذا أنا فيها مقبل على علوم غير مهمة، ولا
نافعة في طريق الآخرة.
ثم تفكرت في نيتي في التدريس، فإذا هي غير خالصة لوجه الله تعالى، بل
باعثها ومحركها طلب الجاه وانتشار الصيت، فتيقنت أني على شفا جرف هار، وأني
قد أشفيت على النار، إن لم أشتغل بتلافي الأحوال. فلم أزل أتفكر فيه مدة،
وأنا بعد على مقام الاختيار، أصمم العزم
على الخروج من بغداد ومفارقة تلك الأحوال يوما، وأحل العزم يوما، وأقدم
فيه رجلا وأؤخر عنه أخرى. لا تصدق لي رغبة في طلب الآخرة بكرة، إلا ويحمل
عليها جلد الشهوة حملة فيفترها عشية، فصارت شهوات الدنيا تجاذبني بسلاسلها
إلى المقام، ومنادي الإيمان ينادي: الرحيل الرحيل! فلم يبق من العمر إلا
قليل، وبين يديك السفر الطويل، وجميع ما أنت فيه من العلم والعمل رياء
وتخييل! فإن لم تستعد الآن للآخرة، فمتى تستعد؟ وإن لم تقطع الآن هذه
العلائق فمتى تقطع؟ فعند ذلك تنبعث الداعية، وينجزم العزم على الهرب
والفرار! ثم يعود الشيطان ويقول: هذه حال عارضة، إياك أن تطاوعها، فإنها
سريعة الزوال، فإن أذعنت لها وتركت هذا الجاه العريض، والشأن المنظوم
الخالي عن التكدير والتنغيص، والأمر المسلم الصافي عن منازعة الخصوم، ربما
التفتت إليه نفسك، ولا يتيسر لك المعاودة.
فلم أزل أتردد بين تجاذب شهوات الدنيا، ودواعي الآخرة، قريبا من ستة أشهر
أولها رجب سنة ثمان وثمانين وأربع مئة، وفي هذا الشهر جاوز الأمر حد
الاختيار إلى الاضطرار، إذ أقفل الله على لساني حتى اعتقل عن التدريس، فكنت
أجاهد نفسي أن أدرس يوما واحدا
تطييبا لقلوب المختلفة إلي، فكان لا ينطلق لساني بكلمة واحدة ولا
أستطيعها البتة، حتى أورثت هذه العقلة في اللسان حزنا في القلب، بطلت معه
قوة الهضم ومراءة الطعام والشراب، فكان لا ينساغ لي ثريد، ولا تنهضم لي
لقمة، وتعدى إلى ضعف القوى، حتى قطع  الأطباء طمعهم من العلاج وقالوا: هذا
أمر نزل بالقلب، ومنه سرى إلى المزاج، فلا سبيل إليه بالعلاج، إلا بأن
يتروح السر عن الهم الملم. ثم لما أحسست بعجزي، وسقط بالكلية اختياري،
التجأت إلى الله تعالى التجاء المضطر الذي لا حيلة له، فأجابني الذي يجبي
المضطر إذا دعاه وسهل على قلبي الإعراض عن الجاه والمال والأهل والولد
والأصحاب، وأظهرت عزم الخروج إلى مكة وأنا أدبر في نفسي سفر الشام حذرا أن
يطلع الخليفة وجملة الأصحاب على عزمي على المقام في الشام، فتلطفت بلطائف
الحيل في الخروج من بغداد على عزم أن لا أعاودها أبدا. واستهدفت لأئمة أهل
العراق كافة، إذ لم يكن فيهم من يجوز أن يكون للإعراض عما كنت فيه سبب
ديني، إذ ظنوا أن ذلك هو المنصب الأعلى في الدين، وكان ذلك مبلغهم من
العلم،
ثم ارتبك الناس في الاستنباطات، وظن من بعد عن العراق، أن ذلك كان
لاستشعار من جهة الولاة، وأما من قرب من الولاة كان يشاهد إلحاحهم في
التعلق بي والانكباب علي، وإعراضي عنهم، وعن الالتفات إلى قولهم، فيقولون:
هذا أمر سماوي، وليس له سبب إلا عين أصابت أهل الإسلام وزمرة أهل العلم.
ففارقت بغداد، وفرقت ما كان معي من المال، ولم أدخر إلا قدر الكفاف، وقوت
الأطفال، وترخصا بأن مال العراق مرصد للمصالح، ولكونه وقفا على المسلمين.
فلم أر في العالم مالا يأخذه العالم لعياله أصلح منه. ثم دخلت الشام، وأقمت
به قريبا من سنتين اشغل الشغل لي إلا العزلة والخلوة، والرياضة والمجاهدة،
اشتغالا بتزكية النفس، وتهذيب الأخلاق، وتصفية القلب لذكر الله تعالى، كما
كنت حصلته من كتب الصوفية. فكنت أعتكف مدة في مسجد دمشق، أصعد منارة المسجد
طول النهار، وأغلق بابها على نفسي، وثم رحلت منها إلى بيت المقدس، أدخل كل
يوم الصخرة، وأغلق بابها على نفسي. ثم تحركت في داعية فريضة الحج،
والاستمداد من بركات مكة
والمدينة وزيارة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بعد الفراغ من زيارة
الخليل صلوات الله وسلامه عليه،  وفسرت إلى الحجاز، ثم جذبتني الهمم، ودعوات
الأطفال إلى الوطن، فعاودته بعد أن كنت أبعد الخلق عن الرجوع إليه، فآثرت
العزلة به أيضا حرصا على الخلوة، وتصفية القلب للذكر.
وكانت حوادث الزمان، ومهمات العيال، وضرورات المعيشة، تغير في وجه
المراد، وتشوش صفوة الخلوة، وكان لا يصفو لي الحال إلا في أقوات متفرقة.
لكني مع ذلك لا أقطع طمعي منها، فتدفعني عنها العوائق، وأعود إليها.
ودمت على ذلك مقدار عشر سنين، وانكشفت لي في أثناء هذه الخلوات أمور لا
يمكن إحصاؤها واستقصاؤها، والقدر الذي أذكره لينتفع به. إني علمت يقينا أن
الصوفية هم السالكون لطريق الله تعالى خاصة وأن سيرتهم أحسن السير، وطريقهم
أصوب الطرق، وأخلاقهم أزكى الأخلاق، بل لو جمع عقل العقلاء، وحكمة الحكماء،
وعلم الواقفين على أسرار الشرع من
العلماء، ليغيروا شيئا من سيرهم وأخلاقهم، ويبدلوه بما هو خير منه، لم
يجدوا إليه سبيلا. فإن جميع حركاتهم وسكناتهم، في ظاهرهم وباطنهم، مقتبسة
من نور مشكاة النبوة، وليس وراء نور النبوة على وجه الأرض نور يستضاء به.
وبالجملة، فماذا يقول القائلون في طريقة، طهارتها - وهي أول شروطها -
تطهير القلب بالكلية عما سوى الله تعالى، ومفتاحها الجاري منها مجرى
التحريم من الصلاة، استغراق القلب بالكلية بذكر الله، وآخرها الفناء
بالكلية في الله؟!
وهذا آخرها بالإضافة إلى ما يكاد يدخل تحت الاختيار والكسب من أوائلها.
وهي على التحقيق أول الطريقة، وما قبل ذلك كالدهليز للسالك إليه. ومن أول
الطريقة تبتدئ المكاشفات والمشاهدات، حتى أنهم في يقظتهم يشاهدون الملائكة،
وأرواح الأنبياء ويسمعون أصواتا ويقتبسون منهم فوائد. ثم يترقى الحال من
مشاهدة الصور والأمثال، إلى درجات يضيق عنها النطق، فلا يحاول معبر أن يعبر
عنها إلا اشتمل لفظه
على خطأ صريح لا يمكنه الاحتراز عنه.
وعلى الجملة، ينتهي الأمر إلى قرب، يكاد يتخيل منه طائفة الحلول، وطائفة
الاتحاد، وطائفة الوصول، وكل ذلك خطأ. وقد بينا وجه الخطأ فيه في كتاب
المقصد الأسنى. بل الذي لابسته تلك الحالة لا ينبغي أن يزيد على أن يقول:
وكان ما كان مما لست أذكره ... فظن خيرا ولا تسأل عن الخبر
وبالجملة فمن لم يرزق منه شيئا بالذوق، فليس يدرك من حقيقة النبوة إلا
الاسم، وكرامات الأولياء، هي على التحقيق، بدايات الأنبياء. وكان ذلك أول
حال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حين أقبل إلى جبل حراء حيث كان يخلو فيه
بربه ويتعبد، حتى قالت العرب: إن محمدا عشق ربه.
وهذه الحالة، يتحققها بالذوق من يسلك سبيلها. فمن لم يرزق الذوق،
فيتيقنها بالتجربة والتسامع، وإن أكثر
الصحبة، حتى يفهم ذلك بقرائن الأحوال يقينا. ومن جالسهم، استفاد منهم هذا
الإيمان فهم القوم لا يشقى جليسهم. ومن لم يرزق صحبتهم فليعلم إمكان ذلك
يقينا بشواهد البرهان، على ما ذكرناه في كتاب عجائب القلب من كتب إحياء
علوم الدين. والتحقيق بالبرهان علم، وملابسة عين تلك الحالة ذوق، والقبول
من التسامح والتجربة بحسن الظن إيمان.
فهذه ثلاث درجات: " يرفع الله الذين أمنوا منكم والذين أوتوا العلم درجات
". ووراء هؤلاء قوم جهال، هم المنكرون لأصل ذلك، المتعجبون من هذا الكلام،
ويستمعون ويسخرون، ويقولون: العجب! إنهم كيف يهذون! وفهيم قال الله تعالى:
" ومنهم من يسمع إليك حتى إذا خرجوا من عندك قالوا للذين أوتوا العلم ماذا
قال آنفا أولئك الذين طبع الله على قلوبهم واتبعوا أهواءهم فأصمهم وأعمى
أبصارهم ".
ومما بان لي بالضرورة من ممارسة طريقتهم، حقيقة النبوة وخاصيتها ولا بد
من التنويه على أصلها لشدة مسيس الحاجة إليها.

- Root: س ل ك (salaka)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To tread, traverse, or enter upon a road; the act of journeying along a path.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The spiritual wayfarer's methodical pursuit of God, entailing both outward discipline and inward purification.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical travel; metaphorical (majāz) for the soul's moral and spiritual itinerary toward the Divine.
- Root: ذ و ق (dhawq)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To taste; the direct perception of flavor.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Immediate, experiential cognition of spiritual realities, distinct from discursive reason (ʿaql) or hearsay (samāʿ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for gustation; transferred to intuitive, unmediated apprehension of divine truths—the hallmark of the Sufi's state (ḥāl).
- Root: خ ل و (khalā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be empty, solitary, or secluded; a place void of others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Seclusion as the precondition for heart-purification (takhliyyah) and the cultivation of presence with God.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for spatial emptiness; metaphorical for the heart's evacuation of all save God.

chapters.translation:
Then, when I had completed these sciences, I turned my whole aspiration (himmatī) to the path of the Sufis (ṭarīq al-ṣūfiyyah). I knew that their way is only perfected through knowledge (ʿilm) and practice (ʿamal). The sum of their sciences was the severing of the soul's impediments (qaṭʿ ʿuqab al-nafs), the purification from its blameworthy traits and vicious qualities—until, by these means, one arrives at emptying the heart of all save God most High (takhliyyah al-qalb ʿan ghayr Allāh) and adorning it with the remembrance of God (taḥliyyah bi-dhikr Allāh).

Now, knowledge was easier for me than practice. So I began by acquiring their knowledge through studying their books—such as the *Qūt al-Qulūb* of Abū Ṭālib al-Makkī (may God have mercy on him), the writings of al-Ḥārith al-Muḥāsibī, and the scattered transmitted sayings of al-Junayd, al-Shiblī, and Abū Yazīd al-Bisṭāmī (may God sanctify their spirits), and other masters—until I came to see the inner core of their intellectual aims and obtained whatever could be obtained of their way through learning and hearing. Then it became clear to me that their most distinctive property is something unattainable by learning, but only by tasting (dhawq), by a state (ḥāl), and by the transformation of attributes. How vast is the difference between knowing the definition of health and satiety, with their causes and conditions, and actually being healthy and sated! And between knowing the definition of intoxication—that it is a condition arising from vapors ascending from the stomach and overwhelming the seat of thought—and actually being drunk! Indeed, the drunkard does not know the definition of intoxication while drunk; he has no knowledge of it at all. The physician, in a state of illness, knows the definition of health, its causes and remedies, while lacking health itself. Likewise, there is a difference between knowing the reality of renunciation (zuhd), its conditions and causes, and your state being that of renunciation—the soul's turning away from the world!

So I knew with certainty that they are the masters of states (arbāb al-aḥwāl), not the possessors of mere sayings (aṣḥāb al-aqwāl). And whatever could be obtained through the path of knowledge, I had obtained it. Nothing remained except what is inaccessible through hearing and learning, but only through tasting and wayfaring (sulūk). Now, there had settled with me—from the sciences I had practiced and the paths I had traversed, in my investigation of both the religious and rational sciences—a certain faith (īmān yaqīnī) in God most High, in prophethood (nubuwwah), and in the Last Day.

These three principles of faith had become firmly rooted in my soul, not through any single specific proof, but through causes, indications, and experiences whose details cannot be enumerated. It had become evident to me that I had no hope of the happiness of the Hereafter except through piety (taqwā) and restraining the soul from caprice (hawā); and that the head of all this is severing the heart's attachment to this world—by withdrawing from the Abode of Delusion (dār al-ghurūr), turning in repentance to the Abode of Eternity (dār al-khulūd), and directing the whole of one's aspiration toward God most High. And that this is not accomplished except by turning away from status (jāh) and wealth (māl), and fleeing from distractions and attachments (shawāghil wa ʿalāʾiq).

Then I examined my own circumstances—and behold, I was immersed in attachments, besieged by them from every side. I examined my works—the best of which was teaching and instruction—and behold, I was engaged in sciences neither important nor useful for the path of the Hereafter.

Then I reflected on my intention (niyyah) in teaching, and behold, it was not pure for the face of God most High; rather, its motive and driver was the pursuit of status and the spread of reputation. So I became certain that I was on the brink of a crumbling precipice (shafā juruf hār), and that I was on the verge of the Fire—if I did not busy myself with repairing my condition. I continued to ponder this for a time, still at the station of choice (maqām al-ikhtiyār): one day resolving firmly to leave Baghdad and forsake those circumstances, the next day dissolving that resolve—advancing one foot and drawing back the other. No sooner would a genuine desire for the Hereafter arise in the morning than the whip of lust would assault it and weaken it by evening. Thus the desires of this world pulled me with their chains toward staying, while the crier of faith cried out: "Departure! Departure!" For little remains of life, and before you lies the long journey; all that you possess of knowledge and practice is pretense and illusion! If you do not prepare now for the Hereafter, when will you prepare? If you do not sever these attachments now, when will you sever them?

At that, the call would surge forth, and the resolve to flee and escape would be firmly sealed. Then Satan would return and say: "This is a passing state—beware of obeying it, for it will quickly vanish. If you yield to it and abandon this vast status, this well-ordered position free of trouble and vexation, this uncontested authority clear of opponents' disputes, perhaps your soul will yearn for it again, and return will not be easy for you."

I continued to oscillate between the tug of worldly desires and the calls of the Hereafter for nearly six months—its beginning being Rajab of the year 488 AH. In that month, the matter passed beyond choice into compulsion (iḍṭirār), for God locked my tongue such that I was prevented from teaching. I would struggle with myself to teach even one day, to gratify the hearts of those who frequented me, but my tongue would not utter a single word—I could not manage it at all. This speechlessness in the tongue wrought a grief in the heart that nullified the power of digestion and the appetite for food and drink. No broth could be swallowed, no morsel digested; it spread to the weakening of my faculties, until the physicians despaired of treatment and said: "This is a matter that has descended upon the heart, and from it spread to the temperament; there is no way to treat it except that the secret (sirr) be relieved of the grief that has befallen it."

Then, when I sensed my incapacity and my choice collapsed entirely, I sought refuge in God most High—the refuge of one compelled who has no recourse. He who answers the compelled when he calls Him answered me, and He made easy for my heart the turning away from status, wealth, family, children, and companions. I announced my resolve to depart for Mecca, while inwardly planning a journey to Syria—fearing that the Caliph and the body of my associates would learn of my intention to remain in Syria. So I employed subtle ruses to leave Baghdad, resolved never to return to it. I became a target of reproach among all the scholars of Iraq, for none of them could conceive that turning away from what I had possessed could have a religious cause—for they supposed that position was the highest rank in religion, and that was the extent of their knowledge.

Then people became entangled in conjectures. Those far from Iraq thought my departure was due to some apprehension concerning the authorities. But those close to the rulers, who witnessed their insistence on clinging to me and their devotion to me—and my turning away from them and disregarding their words—would say: "This is a heavenly matter; its only cause is an evil eye that afflicted the people of Islam and the company of scholars."

So I left Baghdad, distributing all the wealth I had with me, retaining only enough for sustenance and provision for my children—deeming it permissible that Iraqi wealth, being designated for public welfare and endowed for the Muslims, could be taken by a scholar for his family. I saw no wealth in the world more fitting for a scholar to take for his dependents than that.

Then I entered Syria and remained there for nearly two years. My sole occupation was seclusion (ʿuzlah), solitude (khalwah), discipline (riyāḍah), and striving (mujāhadah)—occupying myself with purifying the soul, refining the character, and cleansing the heart for the remembrance of God most High, just as I had learned from the books of the Sufis. I would observe retreat (iʿtikāf) for periods in the Mosque of Damascus, ascending the minaret of the mosque the whole day and locking its door upon myself. Then I departed from there to Jerusalem, entering the Dome of the Rock each day and locking its door upon myself.

Then the call of the obligatory pilgrimage (ḥajj) stirred in me, seeking the blessings of Mecca and Medina and the visitation of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him)—after completing the visitation of Abraham's shrine (peace and blessings of God be upon him). I set out for the Hijaz. Then aspirations and the prayers of my children drew me back to the homeland, though I had been the farthest of people from returning to it. Yet I chose seclusion there as well, eager for solitude and the cleansing of the heart for remembrance.

The vicissitudes of time, the cares of family, and the necessities of livelihood would alter the face of my intention and disturb the purity of my solitude. My state would not be clear except in scattered moments. Yet despite that, I did not cut off my hope from it; obstacles would push me away, and I would return to it.

I continued in this manner for about ten years. During these seclusions, matters were unveiled to me that cannot be enumerated or fully surveyed. What I will mention is for the reader's benefit: I knew with certainty that the Sufis are exclusively the wayfarers upon the path of God most High; that their conduct is the best of conduct, their path the most correct of paths, and their morals the purest of morals. Indeed, were one to gather the intellect of the intelligent, the wisdom of the wise, and the knowledge of those scholars who have penetrated the secrets of the Law, to change something of their conduct and morals and replace it with something better—they would find no way to do so. For all their movements and stillnesses, in their outward and inward aspects, are derived from the light of the niche of prophethood (nūr mishkāt al-nubuwwah); and beyond the light of prophethood there is no light on the face of the earth by which illumination may be sought.

In sum, what can the speakers say about a path whose purity—being its first condition—is the complete purification of the heart from all save God most High; whose key, running in it as the opening takbīr runs in prayer, is the total immersion of the heart in the remembrance of God; and whose end is complete annihilation (fanāʾ) in God?!

And this end is relative to what nearly falls within choice and acquisition from its beginnings. In truth, it is the beginning of the path; what precedes it is like the vestibule for the one entering it. From the very start of the path, unveilings (mukāshafāt) and visions (mushāhadāt) commence—so much so that in their wakefulness they see the angels and the spirits of the prophets, hear voices, and derive benefits from them. Then the state ascends from the vision of forms and likenesses to degrees that speech cannot express. No interpreter attempts to express them without his words containing an evident error from which he cannot guard himself.

In sum, the matter ends in a proximity (qurb) such that one group imagines it to be incarnation (ḥulūl), another union (ittiḥād), and another arrival (wuṣūl)—all of which are errors. We have explained the error in this in the book *al-Maqṣad al-Asnā*. Rather, the one who has experienced that state should not add more than to say:

*"And there was what was—which I do not mention; think well, and ask not for the news."*

In sum, whoever has not been granted something of it through tasting (dhawq) knows nothing of the reality of prophethood except its name. The miracles of the saints (karāmāt al-awliyāʾ) are, in truth, the beginnings of the prophets. Such was the first state of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) when he turned to Mount Ḥirāʾ, where he would seclude himself with his Lord and worship—until the Arabs said: "Muḥammad has fallen in love with his Lord."

This state is verified through tasting by whoever traverses its path. Whoever has not been granted tasting verifies it through experience and hearsay—if he keeps much company with them—until he understands it with certainty through the indications of their states. Whoever sits with them derives this faith from them, for they are a folk whose companion is never wretched. Whoever has not been granted their company should know with certainty the possibility of this through the evidences of demonstration (shawāhid al-burhān), as we have mentioned in the book *ʿAjāʾib al-Qalb* from the *Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn*. Verification through demonstration is knowledge (ʿilm); the direct experience of the very reality of that state is tasting (dhawq); and acceptance through hearsay and experience with good opinion is faith (īmān).

These are three degrees: {«يَرْفَعِ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنكُمْ وَالَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ دَرَجَاتٍ»} ("God will raise those who have believed among you and those who have been given knowledge, by degrees") [Q. 58:11]. Beyond these are ignorant folk who deny the very principle of this, marveling at such speech—they listen and mock, saying: "How strange! How they rave!" Concerning them God most High said: {«وَمِنْهُم مَّن يَسْتَمِعُ إِلَيْكَ حَتَّىٰ إِذَا خَرَجُوا مِنْ عِندِكَ قَالُوا لِلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ مَاذَا قَالَ آنِفًا ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ الَّذِينَ طَبَعَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ وَاتَّبَعُوا أَهْوَاءَهُمْ»} ("And among them are those who listen to you, until when they depart from you, they say to those who have been given knowledge: 'What did he say just now?' Those are the ones whose hearts God has sealed, and who have followed their desires") [Q. 47:16].

And among what became clear to me by necessity from practicing their path is the reality of prophethood and its distinctive property (khāṣṣiyyah). I must touch upon its principle, for the need for it is most pressing.
